extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, scientific researchers, and beginning research students interested in the psychology and methodology of discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for producing and evaluating mathematical (and scientific) discoveries, emphasizing the cognitive stages (preparation, incubation, illumination, later conscious work) and practical recommendations for working, verifying, and fostering insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of invention/discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery involves distinct successive stages: preparation, incubation, illumination, and a fourth later conscious work (verification, precising, continuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly frames discovery as these four stages (Helmholtz and Poincaré): 1) intense preliminary conscious work (preparation); 2) a period where conscious work is set aside and unconscious processes operate (incubation); 3) sudden inspirations or illuminations; 4) a final conscious phase to verify and make precise the result and to continue the work. All stages are necessary and interdependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation stage (intense conscious mobilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation consists of conscious, systematic, often intense work mobilizing relevant ideas and moving elements likely to enter the desired combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation is not useless even when it seems fruitless: it 'launches' elements that the unconscious later recombines. One should direct conscious effort to ideas from which a solution might reasonably be expected. Failure to prepare (or preparing in too narrow a way) undermines chance of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation (set-aside and unconscious recombination)
rubrics_metrics.description: After preparation, a period of dropping the problem allows unconscious processes to combine mobilized elements, producing the conditions for sudden inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incubation often follows days of voluntary effort that seemed unproductive; letting the problem 'sleep' is useful. Empirical questions remain (duration, time-of-day effects) but practical rule: when no further advance seems possible, drop the problem temporarily (provisionally) and plan to resume after an interval (months may be advised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illumination (sudden inspiration not pure chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden solutions (illuminations) appear to consciousness after prior preparation and incubation; they are not simply products of pure chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that illumination depends on prior conscious work. Chance plays a role but cannot substitute for systematic preparation; comparisons (Poincaré's 'hooked atoms' or hunting cartridge scattering) illustrate how directed vs broad projection of ideas affects the usefulness of the resulting meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later conscious work: verification
rubrics_metrics.description: After inspiration there must be a conscious phase to verify whether the intuition corresponds to reality (mathematical proof, numerical check, logical validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is essential because the feeling of certitude accompanying insight may be deceptive. This step belongs to consciousness and may require disciplined calculations, attention and volition. Example: Poincaré emphasizes verification as a main purpose of the fourth stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later conscious work: precising (making the idea precise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unconscious does not usually produce fully formed precise results; the conscious mind must 'precise'—state results exactly and perform the disciplined work to make them rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precising can require substantial effort; inspiration supplies a guiding kernel but effective calculations and exact formulations are the task of conscious work. Anti-pattern: expecting an algebraic calculation to be entirely done unconsciously and finding the result ready on awakening—this does not happen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relay-results (intermediate precise results for continuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce intermediate, precisely stated results (relay-results or relay-formulae) that articulate one stage of research to the next and enable systematic continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relay-results are necessary for continuing research: they must be verified and precised so that subsequent stages can be directed from them. The chapter stresses the structural role of relay-results in mathematical science (e.g., the simple fact about triangles leading to many consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerical and algebraic verification (including numerical checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical discovery often requires algebraic and numerical verification; numerical evaluation of coefficients or observed values can be decisive in identifying correct laws or interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Newton’s identification of universal gravitation relied on numerical checks; verifying formulas by calculation may reveal or settle crucial identifications. Anti-pattern: neglecting numerical verification when it is necessary to identify a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between directed and scattered thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster a balance: neither scatter attention too much across unrelated areas nor overstrain into a single narrowly directed line of work; both extremes can harm discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré and Souriau analogies: projecting ideas narrowly increases useful meetings but risks missing remote, exceptional combinations; projecting them widely increases chance of rare, valuable meetings. Avoid excessive scattering (detrimental) and excessive narrowness (may produce oversight and failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate/influence the unconscious (direct preparation to guide unconscious work)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can 'educate' the unconscious by the way preparation work is done—directing it to certain classes of idea—thereby influencing the unconscious combinations that later arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies include mobilizing ideas from various chapters of science, 'think aside' (Souriau) to prepare unexpected directions, and exposing oneself to diverse fields. The text also mentions more speculative means (psychoanalytic methods suggested by Dr. de Saussure) though details are not developed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to drop-and-resume (practical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: After working on a subject and seeing no further advance, provisionally drop it and resume after an interval (sometimes months); this promotes incubation and later productive use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends this as 'useful advice for every student beginning research.' The drop should be provisional with intention to return, allowing the unconscious to process and for relay-results to mature in fringe-consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive faith in a single idea; be ready to correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dogmatically cling to one idea or principle; be ready to detect and correct errors—errors are frequent, detectable, and often correctable in mathematics, though sometimes a mistaken approach can lead to fruitful developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with experimental sciences where clinging to an idea may produce lasting error. Examples: celebrated exceptions where imperfect proofs led to progress (Riemann/Dirichlet's principle). Also many personal examples of oversight caused by too exclusive focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of misleading physical interpretation or fixed heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical interpretation and generally reliable heuristics can sometimes mislead; be prepared to change approach when they point to blind alleys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author's long attempt at Dirichlet's problem misled by a physical interpretation (potential of simple layer) which was a blind alley; the correct approach used double layer potential. Avoid overreliance on a single heuristic even if generally fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of signs and notations as aids, but do not trust them blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation and algebraic signs help thought and manipulation, but mathematicians must not blindly trust symbolic manipulations; calculations can be faulty and must be checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Souriau's claim that algebraists lose sight of ideas when thinking in signs is only roughly true; mathematicians still must verify algebraic results. Anti-pattern: accepting symbolic outputs without independent checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of mental imagery and words in thought (individual differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought may be accompanied by words, images, nonsense syllables, or no inner verbalization at all; individuals vary, and these differences affect expression and the translation of thought into language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galton's introspections show some think without words, others need words to discover or express. Consequence: some people (e.g., Galton) find it hard to put thoughts into language without effort; others (Max Müller) report thought as inseparable from words. This impacts how results are recorded and communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special case: numerical calculators and unconscious computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some prodigious calculators report unconscious interventions producing numerical or partial algebraic results; this ability is distinct from general mathematical creativity and carries its own psychological peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony (Ferrol, Scripture, Binet) indicates that some calculators obtain results intuitively and later reconstruct the path. Distinguish this phenomenon from general mathematical discovery; beware of confusing memorized methods with unconscious derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce precise enunciation to enable consequences to be drawn
rubrics_metrics.description: A result must be consciously and precisely enunciated before its immediate consequences can be deduced; unconscious grasp does not yield derivable consequences until stated explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses that unless a result is consciously enunciated, deductions (e.g., consequences like similitude) will not follow. This motivates the precising and relay-result practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors and failures can be diagnostically informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures (including paradoxical oversights) often reveal methodological defects (too-narrow attention, insufficient 'thinking aside') and can be corrected or analyzed to improve practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many personal and historical examples show oversight from narrow focus; analyzing such failures helps understand discovery process. Some errors (e.g., imperfect proofs) have at times led to fruitful developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical study of incubation conditions (timing, duration) is useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The phenomenology of incubation (time of day, hours/days between preparation and solution, relation to problem difficulty) deserves empirical study and may inform best practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to a 1932 periodical issue and Dwelshauver’s suggestions: pending research, the practical rule to drop problems temporarily is recommended. The page urges systematic study but provides the provisional working rule described above.
